lead: Two processes sit at opposite ends of the heat-input scale. Laser welding focuses a beam of light to a spot a few tenths of a millimetre wide, reaching power densities a thousand times those of an arc: fast welds, narrow heat-affected zones, little distortion. Cold metal transfer (CMT) is a MIG arc that cuts its own current at every short circuit, giving an almost spatter-free weld at low heat input. Both are chosen for thin sheet, for dissimilar metals and for parts that must not distort — car bodies, battery tabs, instrument panels.
prereq: You need: chapter 4.3 for power density and heat input, and chapter 4.4 for the MIG process that CMT modifies.

sections.h3: Laser welding: a beam squeezed into a small spot

blocks.text: A laser emits light of a single wavelength as a narrow parallel beam. A lens focuses that beam to a spot a few tenths of a millimetre wide. All the beam power lands inside that small spot, so the power density is very high.

blocks.where: q is the power density at the work in W/cm²; P is the laser power reaching the work in W; A is the area of the focused spot in cm².

blocks.text: An arc gives about 10³ to 10⁴ W/cm². A focused laser gives 10⁵ to 10⁷ W/cm², roughly a thousand times more. That one fact explains the rest: the metal melts in microseconds, welding is fast, and so little heat enters that distortion stays small.
The 1 µm beams travel to the work head along a flexible optical fibre. A CO₂ beam cannot, so mirrors steer it.

Two operating modes. Below about 10⁶ W/cm² the surface melts and heat flows inwards by conduction: conduction mode, a shallow rounded weld. Above that, the metal boils. The vapour pushes a narrow hole — the keyhole — down through the melt. The beam reflects inside the hole and is absorbed almost completely, so one pass can penetrate several millimetres. The hole travels with the beam and the melt closes behind it, leaving a deep narrow weld with parallel sides and a small heat-affected zone.

The vapour above the keyhole ionises into a plasma plume. The plume absorbs and defocuses the beam, so a shielding gas — helium, argon or a mixture — blows it aside. The same gas protects the molten metal from air, as in arc welding (chapter 4.4).

sections.h3: What laser welding does well, and what it will not forgive

items: Heat input per millimetre is small, so distortion is small (chapter 4.3).
Travel speed of several metres per minute on 1 mm sheet.
No vacuum, no electrode and no flux; the beam never wears out.
Access from one side only; the beam can even pass through a glass window.

blocks.text: Electron beam welding is the other high-energy-beam process: a focused electron beam instead of light. It penetrates even deeper, but the work must sit inside a vacuum chamber, which limits part size and slows the cycle. A laser needs no vacuum.

Fit-up is the hard limit. There is usually no filler wire, so a gap cannot be bridged; the beam goes through the gap and cuts instead of joining. Edges must be cut clean and clamped tight, with any gap a small fraction of the sheet thickness.

Highly reflective metals resist the beam. Cold aluminium and copper reflect most of the 1 µm light and almost all of the 10.6 µm light. Absorption jumps once the keyhole opens, but starting the weld needs extra power, a tilted head or a darker surface. This is why copper busbars and thin aluminium are harder to weld than steel.

Cost and safety complete the picture: high capital cost, and a Class 4 laser needs an interlocked enclosure, eye protection and fume extraction. A collapsing keyhole can also trap gas and leave porosity.

sections.h3: Cold metal transfer: a MIG arc that switches itself off

blocks.text: Cold metal transfer (CMT) is a modified MIG process. In ordinary MIG the wire is fed forward at a steady speed and the arc runs at high current. When the wire touches the pool, a short circuit forms and the current bursts through the thin bridge of liquid metal until it explodes. That explosion throws spatter and dumps heat into the plate.
CMT removes the explosion by controlling two things at once: the current and the position of the wire.

items: The wire is fed forward and the arc burns at low current, melting the tip into a drop.
The drop touches the pool. The short circuit is sensed within microseconds and the current is cut to near zero.
The wire drive reverses and pulls the wire back. The drop is left in the pool, pulled off by surface tension, not blown off by current.
The wire is fed forward again and the arc re-ignites at low current; the cycle repeats, often more than a hundred times a second.

blocks.text: Because the drop detaches with almost no current flowing, spatter is nearly zero. Because the current is low for most of the cycle, heat input per millimetre is small. The arc stays stable at currents far below normal MIG, so sheets thinner than 1 mm can be joined without burning through.

Uses: thin automotive sheet, aluminium-to-steel joints (the aluminium filler melts and wets the steel without melting it, giving a brazed joint), cladding and repair of worn surfaces, and root passes on pipe. The metal still melts — the name means low heat, not a cold weld.

figure.caption: One CMT cycle. The current is cut and the wire pulled back at the short circuit, so the drop leaves the wire without an explosion; the cycle then repeats.

spec.title: One CMT cycle
spec.aria: A four-block cycle: the arc burns with the wire fed forward, a short circuit cuts the current to near zero, the wire retracts and the drop detaches, then the wire advances and the arc re-ignites, repeating.

examples.question: A 2 kW fibre laser welds 1 mm steel sheet. The focused spot diameter is 0.4 mm and the travel speed is 3 m/min. (a) Find the power density at the work in W/cm². (b) Find the heat input in J/mm. (c) Compare this with the 800 J/mm of the MIG weld in chapter 4.4 and say what the difference means for distortion.
steps: Spot area A = π r² = π × (2 × 10⁻⁴)² = 1.2566 × 10⁻⁷ m².
Power density q = P / A = 2000 W / 1.2566 × 10⁻⁷ m² = 1.59 × 10¹⁰ W/m².
Convert to cm²: 1 m² = 10⁴ cm², so q = 1.59 × 10¹⁰ / 10⁴ = 1.59 × 10⁶ W/cm². This is in the keyhole range (10⁵ to 10⁷ W/cm²).
Heat input H = P / v = 2000 / 0.05 = 40 000 J/m = 40 J/mm.
Ratio = 800 / 40 = 20. The laser puts about twenty times less energy into each millimetre of weld, so the weld cools faster, the heat-affected zone is narrower and distortion is much smaller.
examples.answer: Power density 1.59 × 10⁶ W/cm² (keyhole mode) and heat input 40 J/mm, about 20 times less than the 800 J/mm MIG weld, hence far less distortion.

traps: Cold metal transfer is not a cold weld. The wire and the pool still melt; the name only means the heat input is low.
Power density is not total power. A 2 kW laser carries less total power than a 20 kW arc, yet its power density is a thousand times higher.
A laser weld does not tolerate a loose fit-up. With no filler wire, a gap becomes a cut instead of a joint.
Laser welding needs no vacuum; electron beam welding does. Questions often swap these two.
Unit slip: 1 W/cm² = 10⁴ W/m². Divide W/m² by 10⁴ to reach W/cm², not by 10².

quiz.q: Name two laser sources used for welding and give their wavelengths.
quiz.a: CO₂ gas laser at 10.6 µm and Nd:YAG at 1.06 µm. Fibre lasers emit near 1 µm and are the common choice for sheet metal.

quiz.q: What does the wire do in CMT that it does not do in ordinary MIG?
quiz.a: The wire drive reverses at every short circuit and pulls the wire back, so the drop detaches. In ordinary MIG the wire is fed forward at constant speed all the time.

quiz.q: Why does keyhole mode give a deep, narrow weld with parallel sides?
quiz.a: The power density is high enough to boil the metal. Vapour pressure pushes a narrow hole through the melt, the beam is trapped inside and absorbed by multiple reflections, so penetration is deep. The hole moves with the beam and the melt closes behind it, leaving a narrow parallel-sided weld.

quiz.q: Give two reasons for using a shielding gas in laser welding.
quiz.a: It blows away the plasma plume, which would otherwise absorb and defocus the beam, and it protects the molten pool from oxygen and nitrogen in the air.

quiz.q: A 1.5 kW laser is focused to a spot 0.3 mm in diameter. Find the power density in W/cm².
A 0.8 mm aluminium sheet must be joined to 1 mm steel with almost no distortion and no spatter. Choose between laser welding and CMT, and say why the other is the poorer choice.
quiz.a: CMT, used as CMT brazing with aluminium filler. The current is low for most of the cycle, so the thin sheet does not burn through; the filler bridges the gap; and only the aluminium melts, wetting the steel, so a brazed joint forms with little brittle intermetallic growth. A laser needs tight fit-up, is defeated by the high reflectivity of cold aluminium, and an Al-to-steel fusion weld tends to crack.

quiz.q: Why can a MIG weld bridge a 0.2 mm gap in 1 mm sheet, while an autogenous laser weld of the same sheets cannot?
quiz.a: MIG feeds a filler wire into the arc, and the molten filler fills the gap. An autogenous laser weld adds no metal, so the beam passes through the gap and cuts the sheet instead of joining it. The laser joint therefore needs gap-free clamping.

beyond: Not for the exam. Industry often combines the two ideas: laser-arc hybrid welding runs a laser keyhole and a MIG arc in the same pool, getting deep penetration plus gap tolerance. Scanning laser heads with moving mirrors weld car-body panels without moving the part. CMT is the standard heat source for wire-arc additive manufacturing, where a robot builds a metal part layer by layer. Copper is now welded with blue and green diode lasers, because those wavelengths are absorbed far better than 1 µm light. Search for laser-arc hybrid welding, CMT brazing of aluminium to steel, and blue diode laser copper welding.
